course:
I was scared of a taking a philosophy course at first but had to go for it because I didn't have much options. However, I ended up genuinely enjoying it. The readings were very challenging at times; however, when you actually understand them, especially for topics within your scope of interest, you feel truly enlightened. As a person who enjoys writing, I had fun writing the essays. Monica Hocam also gives good constructive criticism which will actually help you improve the way you deliver your ideas. 
In summary, go for the course if you're ready for the long readings and mental stimulus. It will be tough but definitely worth it because you will learn so much.

If this course were mainly about physics or biology, probably, I would be easily bored but Monica's paper choices touched upon social sciences as well. Therefore, it was engaging and we did A LOT OF discussions, I really liked that!

Monica Hoca was one of the best instructors I had in Bilkent. I previously took Phil 243 and 244 so I thought I had a background in philosophy. However, Monica Hoca was a distinctly different instructor. She urged her students to ask questions, both for theirselves and the topic. She threaded the subjects so lightly that even I, who do not have a scientific background, could understand these complicated subjects and participate in them. 

I learned so much in this course, which was not only on science and its history, but also how these questions were asked and how to approach the philosophy of science. I believe this course should be mandatory rather than 243 and 244. This course teaches how to ask questions. How to approach science. Which is a crucial way to explore one's major in college, even if it's not a scientific field. Monica Hoca was an excellent instructor in it. She has a very humorous approach that makes even the most boring topic interesting. She took these topics in such a light way that it was easy to digest and think about. She sparked questions for us to think and discuss, which was literally exercises for our brains. I found myself leaving every course in more curiosity. I found myself asking similar questions in my major and exercised these more. I hope to see similar instructors like Monica in my time left in Bilkent.

However, there were some that were rather difficult for me or distant since I studied economics; I found myself scared and confused about these topics when I first read them. Then, when I came to class, Monica Hoca studied these subjects so interestingly and clearly that we could talk about them. She encouraged her students to ask questions and discuss them. Sometimes I felt silly for asking such dumb questions. She took them in a kind manner; she answered my questions clearly and tried to further develop my thoughts so we could discuss them. This class was a place where I enjoyed coming, and it was bittersweet to look at the clock and see we had few minutes left. She created an environment for her students to discuss in a safe space and learn. I am forever grateful for her teaching and class. I hope to see more classes with Monica; she is a great philosopher, an excellent instructor, and a wonderful person.

This course is absolutely essential for students of our faculty (İİBF) in that every student has to know at least something about political philosophy if they are to pass.

The single poorest decision regarding this course is the selection of book editions. For instance, there are several versions of Hobbes' Leviathan available, and we, for some reason, use the very old English version. This adds a lot of difficulty to the already difficult course, and contributes nothing. The very few differences there may be in content between the old English and current English versions of these books do not get picked up by undergraduate economics and international relations students anyway.
